name: The Rutherford Gold Foil Experiment
statement: A few alpha particles fired at a thin gold foil bounced almost straight back, revealing the atom's tiny dense nucleus.
statementAccent: revealing the atom's tiny dense nucleus
meaning: The Rutherford gold foil experiment, more properly the Geiger-Marsden experiments, was a series of experiments performed by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under the direction of Ernest Rutherford at the University of Manchester between about 1908 and 1913, which revealed the structure of the atom. A beam of alpha particles, the positively charged particles emitted by radioactive substances, was fired at a very thin sheet of gold foil, and the scattered particles were detected as tiny flashes on a fluorescent screen. According to the then-accepted plum pudding model of the atom, in which positive charge was spread diffusely throughout, the alpha particles should have passed through with only small deflections. Instead, while the vast majority did pass nearly straight through, a small fraction were deflected at large angles, and a very few bounced almost straight back. Rutherford found this astonishing, likening it to firing a large shell at tissue paper and having it come back. To explain the rare large deflections, he proposed in 1911 that almost all of an atom's mass and its positive charge are concentrated in a tiny, dense central nucleus, with the electrons occupying the surrounding mostly empty space. The experiment thus overturned the plum pudding model and established the nuclear model of the atom.
mechanism: The experiment worked by watching how alpha particles scatter when they pass through matter. Alpha particles from a radioactive source were collimated into a narrow beam and directed at an extremely thin gold foil, gold being chosen because it can be beaten into sheets only a few atoms thick. On the far side and around the foil, a screen coated with zinc sulfide produced a faint scintillation, a flash of light, wherever an alpha particle struck, and observers counted these flashes through a microscope at various angles. Most alpha particles passed through the foil with little or no deflection, consistent with an atom that is mostly empty. But a small number were deflected through large angles, and about one in eight thousand was turned back through more than ninety degrees. Such large deflections were impossible under the plum pudding model, in which the atom's positive charge was too spread out to repel an alpha particle sharply. Rutherford reasoned that they could only happen if the alpha particle occasionally came very close to a concentrated positive charge, a tiny massive nucleus, whose intense electric field could reverse the particle's path. From the fraction of particles scattered at each angle he worked out, in 1911, the nuclear model, later confirmed in detail by Geiger and Marsden's 1913 measurements.

examples.text: The vast majority of alpha particles passed through the gold foil nearly undeflected, showing the atom is mostly empty space.
About one in eight thousand alpha particles was deflected through more than ninety degrees, some almost straight back.
Rutherford later said the result was as incredible as firing a fifteen-inch shell at tissue paper and having it come back at you.

whyItMatters: The Rutherford gold foil experiment is one of the most consequential experiments in the history of physics, because it revealed the basic structure of the atom. By showing that a small fraction of alpha particles fired at a thin foil were deflected at large angles or bounced back, it demonstrated that the atom is not a diffuse ball of charge, as the plum pudding model held, but consists mostly of empty space with nearly all its mass and positive charge concentrated in a tiny central nucleus. This nuclear model, which Rutherford proposed in 1911, overturned the prevailing picture and became the foundation for the Bohr model of 1913 and for all of modern atomic and nuclear physics. It opened the way to understanding the nucleus, radioactivity, and eventually nuclear energy, and it stands as a classic example of how a careful, quantitative experiment can overturn an accepted theory through a single unexpected result. The image of alpha particles rebounding from unseen nuclei reshaped how scientists conceive of matter itself. As the experiment that discovered the atomic nucleus, it remains a cornerstone of physics.

working.text: direct a narrow beam of alpha particles at an extremely thin sheet of gold.
detect the flashes where scattered particles strike a fluorescent screen at many angles.
from the rare large deflections conclude that a tiny, dense, positive nucleus holds the atom's mass and charge.

limits: The Rutherford gold foil experiment was a series of experiments spanning roughly 1908 to 1913, not a single event, with Geiger and Marsden's discovery of large-angle scattering published in 1909, Rutherford's nuclear model proposed in 1911, and the detailed confirmation of his scattering formula in 1913, so dates and attribution should be given carefully; the hands-on work was Geiger and Marsden's under Rutherford's direction. The famous tissue-paper quotation comes from a 1936 recollection by Rutherford, not a contemporaneous 1909 statement, and its exact wording varies between sources. The nuclear model it established was itself soon refined, since Rutherford's atom did not explain why orbiting electrons do not spiral into the nucleus, a problem addressed by the Bohr model and later quantum mechanics. So the experiment robustly revealed the atomic nucleus, understood as a series of careful measurements whose model was a crucial step later refined by quantum theory.
misreadings: The Rutherford gold foil experiment was not a single dramatic test but a series of experiments over several years, and the hands-on work was Geiger and Marsden's under Rutherford's direction. The nuclear model it established was not the final word, since it could not explain the stability of electron orbits and was refined by the Bohr model and quantum mechanics. And the vivid tissue-paper quote was a later recollection, not a contemporaneous remark, so treating the experiment as one event, the nuclear model as complete, or the quote as spoken in the moment, misreads a landmark series of measurements that discovered the nucleus.
origin: A series of experiments by Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden under Ernest Rutherford at the University of Manchester between about 1908 and 1913, whose large-angle alpha scattering led Rutherford to the nuclear model of the atom in 1911.
